title: Log lines into fields
summary: Parse access logs and app logs with named groups, count requests by status, find the slowest ones, and the shell one-liners seniors use during an incident.

steps.title: A log line is a record in disguise
body: During an incident the question is never "show me the log". It is "how many 502s since 09:12, and which paths?".
To answer it you turn each line into fields. A regex with **named groups** does that in one pass.
Below is the nginx/Apache *combined* log format. Three habits make the pattern robust:
- **Anchor** with `^`, so the engine tries one position per line instead of every position.
- Use **negated classes** for delimited fields: `\[(?<time>[^\]]+)\]` means "everything up to the closing bracket".
It cannot run past the bracket, so it is both correct and fast.
- **Name** the groups (`(?<status>...)`), so the code reads `m.Groups["status"]`, not `m.Groups[6]`, and adding a group
later does not shift every number.
Click a match to see each group. Try breaking a line and watch it stop matching.

steps.prompt: A teammate wrote `\[(?<time>.*)\]` for the timestamp instead of `\[(?<time>[^\]]+)\]`. On which line does it capture the wrong text?
options: Line 2: the greedy `.*` runs on to the last `]` on the line, inside the path
Line 3: the user name `bob` confuses it
Line 1: `.*` cannot match the `+` in the offset
None: both patterns always capture the same text
steps.explain: `.*` is greedy: it grabs the rest of the line and backs off only to the **last** `]`, which on line 2 is in `tags[]`. The negated class `[^\]]+` stops at the first `]`. It is also faster: no backing off at all.

steps.title: Parse the app log
prompt: Your service writes one line per request: time, method, path, status and duration.
```text
09:12:04 GET /api/orders 200 34ms
Write a pattern that matches a whole line, with the named groups `time`, `method`, `path`, `status` and `ms`.
The time is `hh:mm:ss` (two ASCII digits each), the method is capital letters, the path starts with `/` and has no
spaces, the status is exactly three digits, and `ms` is the number before the literal `ms`.
hints: Build it field by field with single spaces between them: `(?<time>...) (?<method>...) (?<path>...) ...`.
steps.explain: Each field has a precise class: digits for numbers, `[A-Z]+` for the method, `\S*` for a path that cannot contain the separator. Precise classes reject garbage lines instead of capturing nonsense from them.

A group's `Value` is always a string: parse it before comparing. Asking for a group name the pattern does not have does not throw; you get a group whose `Success` is false. That is why a typo in a group name fails silently: test your parser.

steps.prompt: Arrange the loop that counts requests per status. Lines that do not parse are skipped.
steps.explain: Match, check `Success`, then read the groups. Reading `m.Groups["status"].Value` on a failed match gives an empty string, and `int.Parse("")` throws.

steps.title: Count requests by status
prompt: Write `string StatusSummary(string[] lines)` for the app log format of the previous steps
(`09:12:04 GET /api/orders 200 34ms`).
Return the count per status, **sorted by status**, then the number of lines that did not parse:
```text
Always count skipped lines. A parser that silently drops lines hides the day the log format changes: your 502 count
drops to zero and the dashboard looks healthy. A rising `skipped` number is how you notice.
Build the `Regex` once, before the loop, and anchor it with `^` and `$`. A `SortedDictionary<int, int>` keeps the
statuses in order.
template: Dojo.Eq("counts per status, sorted, then skipped", "200=3 404=1 502=2 skipped=1", StatusSummary(dojoLog));
Dojo.Eq("a lower-case method does not parse", "301=1 skipped=1", StatusSummary(new[] { "09:12:10 get /x 200 1ms", "09:12:11 GET /x 301 1ms" }));

require.message: Reads the status from a named group

hints: Reuse your pattern from the regex step, wrapped in `^...$`. On `!m.Success`, add one to `skipped` and `continue`.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: slicing logs and data files from the shell
steps.body: When the incident call has started you rarely write a program first. You slice the file on the box with these, and write code only for what you will run again.

toolkit.what: awk splits each line on whitespace into $1, $2, ... In the combined log format $9 is the status and $7 the path.
flags: split on a comma (or any separator) instead of whitespace
the last field; $0 is the whole line
a condition: run the block only on matching lines
toolkit.example: awk '$9 >= 500 {print $7}' access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head
toolkit.when: quick counts on a server, over SSH, during an incident

toolkit.what: Pick columns from simply delimited text. It knows nothing about quotes, so a quoted "Acme, Inc." shifts every column after it (awk -F, has the same flaw).
toolkit.when: TSV, /etc/passwd style files, CSV you know has no quoted fields

toolkit.what: Extract just one capture group from every match across many files, then count the values.
flags: print this replacement instead of the match: here, group 1
no file names in front of the lines
toolkit.when: key=value logs, extracting ids, counting distinct values

toolkit.what: Query structured JSON logs (one JSON object per line). Never regex JSON: field order, spacing and escaping are not fixed.
flags: print strings raw, without JSON quotes
compact output, one object per line
slurp: read every line into one array first
keep only objects where the condition is true
toolkit.when: Serilog, OpenTelemetry or cloud logs exported as JSON lines

toolkit.what: A real CSV parser in PowerShell: quoted fields, embedded commas and doubled quotes all work, and each row becomes an object with a property per column.
flags: a different separator (European exports often use ;)
column names when the file has no header row
the same for JSON; in PowerShell 7 each piped line of a .jsonl file becomes one object
count per group without keeping the rows
toolkit.example: Get-Content .\app.jsonl | ConvertFrom-Json | Group-Object status -NoElement | Sort-Object Count -Descending
toolkit.when: on Windows machines and build agents

toolkit.what: PowerShell's grep returns match objects, so named groups are right there: $_.Matches[0].Groups['s'].Value.
flags: every match on a line, not only the first
toolkit.when: counting by a field on Windows, without writing a script

steps.prompt: Match each option to what it does.
pairs: split fields on commas instead of whitespace
the last field of the line
print only capture group 1 of each match
count runs of identical adjacent lines, so sort first
print strings raw, without JSON quotes
count per group without keeping the objects
steps.explain: `uniq` only collapses lines that are next to each other, which is why every counting pipeline is `sort | uniq -c | sort -rn`.

steps.prompt: Complete the pipeline: the five most common status codes across every file in `logs/`, most common first.
code: rg -o -I __1__ '$1' 'status=(\d{3})' logs/ | sort | uniq __2__ | sort __3__ | head -5
steps.explain: `-r '$1'` prints only the status digits, `uniq -c` puts a count in front of each value, and `sort -rn` sorts those counts as numbers, largest first. Plain `sort -n` would put the least common first.

steps.title: The slowest requests
prompt: The incident lead asks: "what were the slowest requests?" Write `List<string> SlowestRequests(string[] lines, int n)`.
Parse each line in the same format, skip lines that do not parse, and return the `n` slowest requests, slowest first,
each formatted as `METHOD path 1234ms`:
```text
POST /api/payments 2210ms
POST /api/checkout 1834ms
GET /api/search 987ms
Careful: the `ms` group is a **string**. Sorted as text, `"987"` comes before `"2210"`. Parse it to an `int` first.
LINQ's `OrderByDescending` and `Take` make this short.
template: Dojo.Eq("the three slowest, slowest first", new List<string> { "POST /api/payments 2210ms", "POST /api/checkout 1834ms", "GET /api/search 987ms" }, SlowestRequests(dojoLog, 3));
Dojo.Eq("the slowest one", new List<string> { "POST /api/payments 2210ms" }, SlowestRequests(dojoLog, 1));
Dojo.Eq("n larger than the log gives every parsed request", 6, SlowestRequests(dojoLog, 10).Count);
Dojo.Eq("no lines, no requests", new List<string>(), SlowestRequests(new string[0], 3));

require.message: Sorts the duration as a number

hints: `lines.Select(line => logLine.Match(line)).Where(m => m.Success)` gives the parsed lines.
